Hence the phrase, “Zhen Shiyin, in a Dream, Perceives the Spiritual Jade.” But what events does this book record, and why was it written? He further says: “Now, after bustling uselessly through the dusty world and accomplishing nothing, I suddenly recall all the young women I once knew. Considering each of them closely, I find that in conduct and understanding they all surpassed me. How could I, a proud and able-bodied man, have proved inferior to those women? My shame is more than ample, yet regret is of no avail—what utter helplessness! At such a time, I resolved to set down a record and tell everyone beneath heaven of my guilt: though I once relied above on Heaven’s favor and below on my ancestors’ virtue, passing my days in brocade as a pampered young gentleman and feasting on rich food, I betrayed my parents’ nurturing kindness and failed the instruction of my teachers and elder companions, until today I have achieved nothing and squandered half my life in adversity. I cannot escape my own guilt; yet the women of the inner chambers truly included remarkable individuals. On no account should my unworthiness and desire to hide my faults cause them to vanish into oblivion as well. p.src: Long ago, when the goddess Nüwa smelted stones to repair the sky, she fashioned at the Incredible Crag in the Great Waste Mountains thirty-six thousand five hundred and one unhewn stones, each twelve zhang high and twenty-four zhang square. The goddess used only thirty-six thousand five hundred of them. One alone remained unused and was cast aside beneath Green Ridge Peak on that mountain. Unexpectedly, after being tempered in the furnace, this stone had acquired spiritual awareness. Seeing all the other stones used to repair the sky while it alone was deemed unworthy and rejected, it lamented its fate, wailing day and night in sorrow and shame.

p.src: One day, while it was still lamenting, it suddenly saw a Buddhist monk and a Taoist priest approaching from afar. Both were extraordinary in bearing and singular in appearance. Talking and laughing, they came to the foot of the peak, sat beside the stone, and began an animated conversation. At first they spoke of mist-shrouded mountains, vast seas, immortals, and mystical wonders; later their talk turned to worldly splendor, rank, and wealth. Hearing this, the stone’s worldly desires were stirred, and it too longed to enter the human realm and savor its glory and wealth. Yet ashamed of its coarse stupidity, it had no choice but to speak in a human voice to the monk and Taoist: “Masters, your disciple is but a clumsy object and cannot properly pay his respects. I have just heard you speak of the splendor and prosperity of the human world, and I yearn for it with all my heart. Though your disciple’s substance is coarse and stupid, I possess some understanding. Moreover, judging from your immortal bearing, neither of you can be an ordinary being: surely you have the ability to mend heaven and aid the world, and the virtue to benefit all creatures and save humankind. If you would show me a little compassion and take your disciple into the dusty world, allowing me to enjoy a few years amid wealth and honor in that land of tenderness, I shall cherish your boundless favor forever and never forget it through ten thousand ages.” When the two immortals had heard him out, they both laughed ingenuously. “Excellent! Excellent! The dusty world does indeed offer certain pleasures, but they can never be relied upon forever. Besides, ‘nothing is perfect’ and ‘good things are beset by troubles’ are eight words forever bound together. In an instant joy gives birth to sorrow, people depart and circumstances change; in the end all is but a dream, and every scene returns to emptiness. Better not to go at all.” But the stone’s worldly passion was already ablaze, and it could not heed these words; it pleaded bitterly again and again. Realizing that it could not be restrained, the two immortals sighed. “This too is fate: after perfect stillness comes the desire for movement, and something arises from nothing. Since you insist, we shall take you to enjoy it—but when disappointment comes, be sure not to regret your choice.” “Of course, of course,” replied the stone. The monk then said, “You may possess spiritual awareness, but your substance is so coarse and stupid, and there is nothing rare or precious about you. As you are, you could serve only as a footstool. Very well. I shall now exert the full power of the Buddha’s law to help you. When this destined age ends, you shall return to your original substance and bring the matter to a close. What do you say?” The stone heard this and thanked him profusely. The monk chanted an incantation, traced a talisman, and displayed his mighty magic. In an instant he transformed the great rock into a piece of lustrous, flawless jade and shrank it to the size of a fan pendant, small enough to hold or wear. Holding it in his palm, the monk laughed. “In form, at least, you have become a treasure! But you still have no practical virtue. I must engrave a few words upon you, so that anyone who sees you will know at once that you are a marvelous object. Then I shall take you to settle and prosper in a flourishing realm of enlightenment, among a clan adorned with poetry, rites, official caps, and hairpins, in a land of brocaded splendor, a home of tenderness, rank, and wealth.” The stone was unable to contain its delight. “What marvelous qualities will your disciple possess, and where will you take me?

p.src: The Taoist Kongkong therefore said to the Stone, “Brother Stone, according to your own account this story of yours possesses a certain interest, and so you have set it down here in hopes that it may be published as a marvel. Yet as I see it, first, no dynasty or date can be established; second, it contains no worthy sages or loyal ministers whose wise government ordered the court and reformed society. There are merely a few unusual young women—some passionate, some infatuated, some possessed of modest talents or minor virtues—yet none has the moral worth or ability of Ban Zhao or Cai Wenji. Even if I copied it out, I fear people would not care to read it.” The Stone replied with a laugh, “Master, why are you so foolish? If the absence of a verifiable dynasty troubles you, how difficult would it be for you simply to borrow the dates of the Han or Tang and embellish the story with them? But it seems to me that unofficial histories throughout the ages have all followed the same worn path. My refusal to borrow that convention makes this work fresh and distinctive instead. It is the substance of the events and the truth of human feelings that matter; why be so rigidly bound to dynasties and dates? Besides, among ordinary townsfolk, very few enjoy books on government and moral order, while a great many delight in light reading that entertains. Unofficial histories of former times either slander sovereigns and ministers or defame other men's wives and daughters; their treachery, lust, violence, and wickedness are beyond counting. There is also a species of writing devoted to amorous affairs, so obscene and foul that it poisons the written word and corrupts the young; such works too are beyond counting. As for books about gifted scholars and beautiful ladies, a thousand volumes all issue from the same mold, and none can avoid lapsing into wanton excess. Their pages teem with Pan An, Cao Zhi, Xi Shi, and Zhuo Wenjun. The author merely wishes to display a pair of love poems or florid rhapsodies of his own, so he invents names for a man and a woman, then inevitably introduces a villain to sow trouble between them, like the clown in a play. Even the maids open their mouths only to spout archaic particles, speaking either in literary flourishes or in moral maxims. Read one after another, they are all self-contradictory and grossly contrary to human nature. They cannot compare with these few women whom I saw and heard with my own eyes and ears over half a lifetime. I would not presume to say that they surpass every character in earlier books, but the full course of their lives may dispel sorrow and relieve boredom; and there are also a few clumsy verses and familiar sayings fit to provoke laughter and accompany wine. As for partings and reunions, sorrow and joy, prosperity and decline, and the fortunes that befell them, I have followed every trace of what occurred and dared not introduce the slightest fabrication merely to please the reader's eye at the cost of the story's true transmission. Nowadays the poor are burdened daily by the need for food and clothing, while the rich remain tormented by desires yet unsatisfied. Even when they have a little leisure, they pursue lust and beauty, crave possessions, and go seeking troubles. Where could they find time to read books about government and moral order? Thus I neither wish the world to praise this story as marvelous and sublime, nor insist that people should delight in examining it. I ask only that, when they have had their fill of wine and pleasure and lie down to rest, or when they seek refuge from the world and relief from sorrow, they take it up for diversion. Would that not spare them some portion of their allotted years and bodily strength? Compared with plotting after empty illusions and chasing delusions, it would also spare them the harm of disputes and slander, and the hardship of running themselves off their feet.

p.src: After hearing this, the Taoist Kongkong pondered for a long while and read through The Story of the Stone once more. He saw that although it contained words denouncing treachery and sycophancy, condemning evil and punishing wickedness, their purpose was not to rail against the age or revile society. Wherever it touched upon human relations—benevolent rulers, virtuous ministers, loving fathers, and filial sons—it bestowed praise and celebrated virtue with inexhaustible devotion, and truly could not be compared with other books. Though love was its principal theme, it did no more than faithfully record actual events; it could not be compared with fabricated and extravagant works devoted solely to lewd assignations, secret vows, and clandestine unions. Since it did not interfere in the affairs of the age at all, he copied it from beginning to end and brought it into the world as a marvelous tale. From that time on, the Taoist Kongkong beheld form through emptiness, from form engendered passion, transmitted passion into form, and from form awakened to emptiness. He therefore changed his name to the Monk of Passion and retitled The Story of the Stone as The Record of the Monk of Passion. p.src: One day, during the long hours of a sweltering summer afternoon, Shiyin sat idly in his study until his hand grew weary. Casting aside his book, he leaned over the desk to rest awhile and, before he knew it, drifted into a hazy sleep. In his dream he came to a place he could not recognize. Suddenly he saw a monk and a Taoist approaching from the other side, talking as they walked. He heard the Taoist ask, “Where do you intend to take that foolish object you are carrying?” The monk laughed. “Set your mind at ease. A romantic entanglement is now awaiting its resolution, and all those ill-fated lovers have yet to be born into the mortal world. I shall take this opportunity to slip the foolish thing in among them and let it undergo the experience for itself.” The Taoist said, “So those ill-fated lovers are once again about to bring a calamity upon themselves and pass through the mortal world? But where are they destined to descend?” The monk laughed. “The tale is an amusing one—a marvel unheard of through all the ages. Beside the Stone of Three Incarnations on the bank of the Sacred River in the West grew a Crimson Pearl Plant. The Attendant Shenying of the Palace of Red Jade watered it daily with sweet dew, and thus the plant was able to prolong its life. After absorbing the vital essence of heaven and earth and receiving the nourishment of rain and dew, it shed its plant form, assumed a human shape, and cultivated itself into a maiden. All day it roamed beyond the Heaven of Parted Sorrow, eating Honeyed Azure Fruits when hungry and drinking from the Sea of Infused Sorrow when thirsty. Her bearing was uncommon and her features clear and bright; though she was not exceptionally beautiful, there was nevertheless something captivating about her. Yucun could not help staring at her in a daze. The Zhen family’s maid finished gathering the flowers and was about to leave when she suddenly looked up and saw a man inside the window. His headcloth was worn and his clothes old, and though he was plainly impoverished, he had a broad waist, a sturdy back, a wide face and square mouth, with swordlike brows, brilliant eyes, a straight nose, and prominent cheeks. The maid quickly turned away, thinking, “This man is so powerfully built, yet so ragged. He must be that Jia Yucun whom my master often mentions, saying that he wishes to give him assistance but has never found the opportunity. Our family has no other friend or relative in such poverty, so it can be no one else. No wonder my master says that he is not a man destined to remain in straits for long.” With these thoughts, she could not help looking back twice more. Seeing her look back, Yucun imagined that she had taken a fancy to him and was beside himself with delight. He decided that she must be a rare judge of men, a kindred spirit who had recognized him amid the dust of the world. Presently the young servant came in. Yucun learned from him that Shiyin’s visitor was being kept for dinner, and since he could not wait indefinitely, he let himself out by a side passage. The trouble is that at present I have no means whatever to provide for my baggage and traveling expenses. The capital is far away, and I cannot reach it merely by selling calligraphy and composing essays.”
Before he had finished, Shiyin said, “Why did you not tell me sooner?
I have often wished to help you in this way, but whenever we met, you never mentioned the matter, so I did not dare presume.
Now that you have spoken of it, though I am a man of little ability, I still know the difference between righteousness and profit.
Fortunately, the great examination is to be held next year. You should make haste to the capital and try your strength in the spring examination, so that your learning may not go to waste.
Your traveling expenses and all other incidentals are trifling matters; I shall arrange them for you. That way, your mistaken good opinion of me will not have been entirely misplaced!”
He at once ordered a young servant to go inside and quickly wrap up fifty taels of silver and two sets of winter clothes.

Then he added, “The nineteenth is an auspicious day. You may buy passage on a boat and journey west that very day. Once you have spread your wings and soared high, we shall meet again next winter. What could be more delightful?”
Yucun accepted the silver and clothes, offered no more than a brief word of thanks, and made no great matter of it; he simply continued drinking, talking, and laughing.
It was already past the third watch before the two finally parted.
After seeing Yucun off, Shiyin returned to his room and slept until the red sun stood three poles high.

Thinking over the events of the previous night, he decided to write two letters of introduction for Yucun to take to the capital, so that Yucun might call upon some official family and find a place to stay.

But when he sent someone to invite him over, the servant returned and reported, “The monk says Master Jia left for the capital at the fifth watch this morning. He also left a message for the monk to convey to you, sir: ‘A scholar need not heed whether a day is auspicious or inauspicious; what matters is whether the undertaking is reasonable. I had no time to bid you farewell in person.’”
On hearing this, Shiyin had no choice but to let the matter drop.
Truly, in times of leisure the days pass swiftly; in the blink of an eye, the Lantern Festival had come again.

Shiyin ordered his servant Huo Qi to carry Yinglian out to see the festival performances and lanterns. Around midnight, Huo Qi needed to relieve himself, so he set Yinglian down on the threshold of a house.
But when he returned to pick her up, there was no trace of Yinglian.
In desperation, Huo Qi searched throughout the night, but by daybreak he had still not found her. He no longer dared return to face his master and fled to another region.

When Shiyin and his wife saw that their daughter had not returned all night, they knew something was wrong. They sent several more people to search, but all came back saying that there was neither sight nor word of her.
The couple had been blessed with this one daughter alone in half a lifetime. How could they not pine for her when she was suddenly lost? They wept day and night and very nearly took their own lives.

p.src: Then, unexpectedly, on the fifteenth day of the third month, while offerings were being fried in the Gourd Temple, the monks grew careless. Flames leapt from the oil cauldron and set the paper window ablaze. Most houses in that district had bamboo fences and wooden walls. As though calamity had been ordained, the flames spread from one building to the next, catching everywhere, until the whole street blazed like the Mountain of Flames. Although soldiers and townspeople came to fight the blaze, by then it had gathered such force that nothing could be done. It burned through the whole night before gradually dying away, and no one knew how many homes had been consumed. Poor Zhen’s house stood next door and had long since been reduced to a field of rubble. Only he, his wife, and several servants escaped with their lives. In his distress, Shiyin could do nothing but stamp his feet and heave long sighs. He had no choice but to consult his wife and arrange for them to take refuge at their farmstead. Unfortunately, successive years of flood and drought had ruined the harvests, while bands of marauders sprang up everywhere. They seized fields and land, pilfered and plundered, and left the people no peace. Government troops were therefore conducting punitive campaigns, making the countryside impossible to inhabit. Shiyin was forced to sell off all his farmland, and then took his wife and two maidservants to seek refuge with his father-in-law.

p.src: His father-in-law was named Feng Su, a native of Daruzhou. Though a farmer, he was comfortably well-to-do. When he saw his son-in-law arrive in such a wretched state, he was somewhat displeased. Fortunately, Shiyin still had some of the money from the sale of his land. He handed it to Feng Su and asked him to buy, at whatever suitable price he could, a modest house and a little land as provision for their future livelihood. But Feng Su, half coaxing and half cheating him, gave him only a little poor land and a few dilapidated rooms. Shiyin was a scholar, unaccustomed to managing a livelihood or farming. After struggling along for a year or two, he found himself sinking ever deeper into poverty. Whenever Feng Su saw him, he offered nothing but empty platitudes; both in public and in private, he complained that the couple did not know how to manage a household and accused them of caring only to eat well while shirking work. Shiyin realized that he had placed his trust in the wrong man and could not help regretting it bitterly. Moreover, the previous year’s shocks, fright, anger, resentment, and grief had left deep injuries within him. Now advanced in years and assailed by both poverty and illness, he gradually began to show signs that his end was near.

p.src: The humble room stands empty, though once the bed was heaped with courtly tablets; rank weeds and withered poplars cover what was once a hall of song and dance. Cobwebs now cover the carved beams, while green gauze is pasted anew over humble lattice windows. Why boast that rouge is rich and powder fragrant, when in a moment both temples are white with frost? Yesterday, by a mound of yellow earth, one buried white bones; tonight, beneath red lamps and silken curtains, lovers lie entwined. Chests brim with gold, chests brim with silver—then, in the blink of an eye, one becomes a beggar whom all revile. Even as one laments another's short life, who knows that death is already coming home for oneself? Raise a child with the soundest instruction—there is no assurance he will not grow into an outlaw. Choose a husband from a wealthy house—who could foresee her falling into a quarter of courtesans? Coveting a higher official cap, one ends by bearing cangue and shackles. Yesterday one pitied the cold in a ragged coat; today one complains that the purple robe of rank is too long. Amid the clamor, no sooner has one finished singing than another takes the stage, each mistaking a foreign land for home. How absurd! In the end, all are merely sewing wedding clothes for someone else.

Everyone said that the new prefect had arrived to take office. The maid withdrew inside the gate to watch. She saw guards and constables pass by in pairs, and presently a great sedan chair went past, bearing an official in a black cap and scarlet robe. The maid started in surprise, thinking that the official looked very familiar, as though she had seen him somewhere before. Then she went back into the room and put the matter out of her mind. That evening, just as they were about to retire, there suddenly came a tremendous pounding at the gate and many voices shouting in confusion: “His Excellency the Prefect has sent men to summon someone for questioning!” Hearing this, Feng Su was so terrified that he stared speechlessly, not knowing what calamity had befallen him.
